quiz_met4:1.q: A patient's red blood cells are exposed to an oxidant drug, and their glutathione becomes oxidized. Glutathione reductase restores reduced glutathione using which product of glucose oxidation?
quiz_met4:1.r: NADPH from the oxidative phase of the pentose phosphate pathway is what glutathione reductase uses to turn GSSG back into 2 GSH, which the slide marks as important to combat oxidative damage in red blood cells and cornea (p. 687).

quiz_met4:10.q: After intense exercise, a hepatocyte is making glucose mainly from lactate. Where is oxaloacetate converted to phosphoenolpyruvate on this route, and why? LDH is lactate dehydrogenase and PEP is phosphoenolpyruvate.
o: Cytosol, as malate exports the NADH
Cytosol, as LDH uses up cytosolic NADH
Mitochondria, as LDH makes cytosolic NADH
Cytosol, as PEP cannot leave mitochondria
quiz_met4:10.r: On the lactate route, lactate dehydrogenase already generates NADH in the cytosol, so NADH does not need to be shuttled out as malate; mitochondrial PEP carboxykinase makes PEP inside the mitochondrion and PEP leaves (p. 712).

quiz_met4:11.q: A fasting patient's liver is making glucose mainly from alanine. On the lecture's route for this precursor, in what form do the carbons leave the mitochondrion?
quiz_met4:11.r: On the alanine route, mitochondrial malate dehydrogenase reduces oxaloacetate to malate, malate leaves, and cytosolic malate dehydrogenase remakes oxaloacetate and NADH before cytosolic PEP carboxykinase makes PEP (p. 712).

quiz_met4:12.q: A toxin depletes GTP in hepatocytes while leaving ATP normal. Which enzyme of gluconeogenesis is directly unable to act?
quiz_met4:12.r: PEP carboxykinase uses GTP to convert oxaloacetate to PEP. Pyruvate carboxylase uses ATP, and the two phosphatases only add water and release Pi (p. 711).

quiz_met4:13.q: Two fasting children are each given an alanine infusion. In the child with a glucose 6-phosphatase defect, blood glucose does not rise. In the child with a liver glycogen phosphorylase defect, it rises. Which statement about hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis explains the difference?
o: Phosphorylase is needed to export glucose
Alanine is converted to glycogen first
quiz_met4:13.r: Glucose 6-phosphatase is the last step for glucose from both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, so its loss blocks release of all glucose from the liver (p. 703, p. 717). A phosphorylase defect only blocks G1P from glycogen, and glucose can still be made by gluconeogenesis (p. 717).

quiz_met4:14.q: During an overnight fast, glucagon acts on a patient's liver. According to the lecture, which combination of hepatic enzyme activities results? FBPase-1 is fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase.
o: PFK-1 on, pyruvate kinase on, FBPase-1 off
PFK-1 off, pyruvate kinase off, FBPase-1 on
PFK-1 off, pyruvate kinase on, FBPase-1 on
PFK-1 on, pyruvate kinase off, FBPase-1 on
PFK-1 off, pyruvate kinase off, FBPase-1 off
quiz_met4:14.r: In liver, glucagon and epinephrine lower glycolysis and raise gluconeogenesis: the slide note reads inactive PFK-1, inactive pyruvate kinase, active fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase (p. 705).

quiz_met4:15.q: After a carbohydrate meal, insulin causes dephosphorylation of the bifunctional enzyme PFK-2/FBPase-2 in hepatocytes. What follows? F2,6BP is fructose 2,6-bisphosphate.
quiz_met4:15.r: Insulin acts through a phosphoprotein phosphatase; the dephosphorylated enzyme has PFK-2 active and FBPase-2 inactive, so F2,6BP rises (p. 716). F2,6BP activates PFK-1 and inhibits FBPase-1, which stimulates glycolysis and inhibits gluconeogenesis (p. 715).

quiz_met4:16.q: In a cell whose energy supply is falling, AMP rises. According to the lecture, which pair of allosteric effects does AMP have?
o: Inhibits PFK-1, no effect on FBPase-1
quiz_met4:16.r: AMP activates PFK-1 and inhibits FBPase-1, so it pushes glycolysis and holds back gluconeogenesis. ADP also activates PFK-1; ATP and citrate inhibit it (p. 713).

quiz_met4:17.q: Purified PFK-1 is assayed at increasing fructose 6-phosphate concentrations. At high ATP the activity curve shifts to the right, even though ATP is also a substrate of the enzyme. According to the lecture, how does ATP produce this inhibition?
o: Competes with substrate at the active site
Depletes the AMP in the assay
quiz_met4:17.r: PFK-1 has an active site and a separate allosteric site. ATP is a substrate at the active site and an allosteric inhibitor, so high ATP shifts the curve right; AMP, ADP and F2,6BP activate, citrate inhibits (p. 714).

quiz_met4:18.q: During an all-out 200 m sprint, working muscle becomes anaerobic. According to the lecture, which property of fat makes glycogen the necessary fuel store here?
o: Fatty acids cannot enter muscle cells
Fat is less energy dense than glycogen
Fatty acids cannot be used anaerobically
Fatty acids are converted to glucose first
Fatty acids cannot be stored in muscle
quiz_met4:18.r: Fat is more energy-dense, but fatty acids cannot be metabolized anaerobically, muscles cannot use fat as rapidly as glycogen, and animals cannot convert fatty acids to glucose (p. 693).

quiz_met4:19.q: An enzyme that removes glucose residues only from non-reducing ends is added to a single glycogen molecule and works at many sites at once. Which structural feature of glycogen allows this?
o: Each chain ends in a reducing end
Alpha-1,6 branches give many such ends
Glycogenin is attached to every chain
Alpha-1,4 linkages occur at branch points
quiz_met4:19.r: Glycogen has alpha-1,4 linkages with alpha-1,6 branch points. Extensive branching gives one molecule many non-reducing ends but only a single reducing end, which is attached to glycogenin (p. 691).

quiz_met4:2.q: Cultured hepatocytes are treated with drugs that block fatty acid synthesis, sterol synthesis and glutathione reductase. Entry of glucose 6-phosphate into the pentose phosphate pathway then falls. Which mechanism explains the fall?
quiz_met4:2.r: NADPH feedback-inhibits the first step of the pathway, glucose 6-phosphate to 6-phosphogluconolactone (p. 688). The blocked reactions are the ones that consume NADPH (p. 687), so NADPH builds up and closes entry.

quiz_met4:20.q: After a meal, radiolabeled glucose is traced into liver glycogen. Which labeled molecule is the immediate glucose donor used by glycogen synthase?
quiz_met4:20.r: Glycogen synthase transfers glucose from UDP-glucose to the non-reducing end of an existing chain and releases UDP (p. 696). Glucose 6-phosphate and glucose 1-phosphate are earlier intermediates (p. 694).

quiz_met4:21.q: A cell lacks inorganic pyrophosphatase, and pyrophosphate builds up during glycogen synthesis. Which step generates this pyrophosphate? G1P is glucose 1-phosphate and G6P is glucose 6-phosphate.
quiz_met4:21.r: Glucose activation joins a sugar phosphate to an NTP to give the sugar nucleotide (UDP-glucose) plus pyrophosphate, which inorganic pyrophosphatase splits to 2 Pi (p. 694); the pathway map draws glucose 1-phosphate going to UDP-glucose (p. 717). Glycogenin and glycogen synthase release UDP, not pyrophosphate (p. 695, p. 696).

quiz_met4:22.q: A cell line lacking glycogenin has normal glycogen synthase and normal UDP-glucose levels, yet it starts no new glycogen molecules. Why can glycogen synthase not begin a chain by itself?
o: It adds only to the single reducing end
It needs a chain longer than 4 residues
quiz_met4:22.r: Glycogen synthase only extends the non-reducing end of an existing chain with more than 4 residues (p. 696). Glycogenin makes that primer on its own Tyr194 from UDP-glucose, repeating six times (p. 695).

quiz_met4:23.q: A child's liver biopsy shows glycogen with very long unbranched chains and almost no alpha-1,6 linkages. Which enzyme is most likely deficient?
quiz_met4:23.r: Glycogen-branching enzyme moves a block of residues from the non-reducing end of an alpha-1,4 chain to create an alpha-1,6 branch point (p. 697). Debranching enzyme removes branches during breakdown (p. 701).

quiz_met4:24.q: A patient's muscle can neither route glucose 6-phosphate into glycogen synthesis nor pass glucose 1-phosphate from glycogen breakdown into glycolysis. A single enzyme is deficient. Which one?
quiz_met4:24.r: Phosphoglucomutase works in both directions: G6P to G1P for synthesis (p. 694) and G1P to G6P after glycogen phosphorylase in breakdown (p. 700).

quiz_met4:25.q: Purified glycogen phosphorylase is incubated with glycogen in a buffer that contains no ATP, and breakdown proceeds normally. What does the enzyme use to cleave each bond, and what is released? G1P is glucose 1-phosphate and G6P is glucose 6-phosphate.
quiz_met4:25.r: Glycogen phosphorylase uses inorganic phosphate, not ATP, to remove the residue at the non-reducing end as glucose 1-phosphate; phosphoglucomutase then converts G1P to G6P (p. 700).

quiz_met4:26.q: Purified glycogen is incubated with only glycogen phosphorylase and debranching enzyme. Most of the product is glucose 1-phosphate, but a small amount of free glucose also appears. Which activity releases the free glucose?
o: Phosphorylase acting at a branch point
Phosphorylase acting at the reducing end
quiz_met4:26.r: Debranching enzyme has two activities: its transferase moves a block of residues, and its alpha-1,6 glucosidase releases the single branch-point residue as free glucose. Phosphorylase is only active five or more residues from a branch point (p. 701).

quiz_met4:27.q: In a muscle extract, protein kinases phosphorylate both glycogen synthase and glycogen phosphorylase. What is the resulting activity of each enzyme?
quiz_met4:27.r: Phosphorylation has opposite effects: phosphorylase b kinase turns phosphorylase b into active phosphorylase a, while GSK3 turns active synthase a into inactive synthase b. PP1 reverses both (p. 706).

quiz_met4:28.q: After a carbohydrate meal, portal blood glucose rises and glucose binds the allosteric sites of liver glycogen phosphorylase a. According to the lecture, what happens to the enzyme next?
o: GSK3 phosphorylates it to phosphorylase b
It becomes more active as phosphorylase a
CKII primes it for further activation
PP1 dephosphorylates it to phosphorylase b
quiz_met4:28.r: Liver glycogen phosphorylase is a glucose sensor: when 2 glucose bind phosphorylase a, phosphorylase a phosphatase (PP1), stimulated by insulin, removes its phosphates and leaves the less active phosphorylase b (p. 704).

quiz_met4:29.q: An isolated muscle is stimulated to contract in a bath with no hormones, and glycogen breakdown accelerates. Which signals activate phosphorylase b kinase in this setting?
quiz_met4:29.r: In muscle, phosphorylase b kinase is activated by epinephrine, raised Ca2+ and raised AMP; in liver it is activated by glucagon. The kinase converts phosphorylase b to active phosphorylase a (p. 706).

quiz_met4:3.q: A patient with severe thiamine deficiency has red blood cells that make NADPH normally but cannot interconvert sugar phosphates in the nonoxidative phase of the pentose phosphate pathway. Which enzyme has lost its cofactor?
quiz_met4:3.r: Transketolase requires thiamine (B1). Transketolase and transaldolase are the two enzymes of the nonoxidative phase, but only transketolase is marked as needing thiamine (p. 687).

quiz_met4:30.q: After a meal, insulin shifts glycogen synthase toward its active form. According to the lecture, by which two actions?
quiz_met4:30.r: Insulin inhibits GSK3, the kinase that inactivates synthase, and activates PP1, the phosphatase that restores active synthase a. Glucose and glucose 6-phosphate also activate PP1; glucagon and epinephrine inhibit it (p. 706).

quiz_met4:4.q: A rapidly dividing tumor cell line has far higher pentose phosphate pathway flux than quiescent cells of the same tissue. According to the lecture, which needs of growing cells explain this?
o: ATP for ion pumps and contraction
NADH for the electron transport chain
Ribose for DNA and NADPH for lipids
quiz_met4:4.r: The pathway's products are NADPH and ribose 5-phosphate. Ribose feeds nucleotides, coenzymes, DNA and RNA, and NADPH feeds reductive biosynthesis of fatty acids and sterols; both carry the note 'higher requirement in cells undergoing rapid growth' (p. 687).

quiz_met4:5.q: A fasting patient is breaking down adipose triacylglycerol and muscle protein. Which of the following products of this breakdown can the liver use as a carbon source for new glucose?
quiz_met4:5.r: Glycerol is a primary gluconeogenic substrate, entering as DHAP. Fatty acids are not substrates because mammals cannot convert acetyl-CoA to pyruvate, and Lys and Leu are the two amino acids excluded from the glucogenic list (p. 709).

quiz_met4:6.q: During a prolonged fast, a patient's hepatocytes oxidize fatty acids at a high rate while making glucose. According to the lecture, what does fatty acid oxidation contribute to gluconeogenesis?
quiz_met4:6.r: Fatty acids are not substrates for gluconeogenesis, but beta-oxidation of fatty acids provides the energy required to drive it (p. 709).

quiz_met4:7.q: During a sprint, anaerobic muscle converts one glucose to two lactate, and the liver converts the two lactate back to one glucose. According to the lecture, how many ATP does the liver spend to make this glucose?
quiz_met4:7.r: The Cori cycle slide draws 6 ATP used by hepatic gluconeogenesis from 2 lactate, against only 2 ATP gained by glycolysis in the peripheral cell (p. 710).

quiz_met4:8.q: A fasting infant has hypoglycemia. Liver cells have normal glycolytic enzymes but cannot convert pyruvate to phosphoenolpyruvate. Which pair of enzymes normally carries out this bypass of pyruvate kinase? PEP is phosphoenolpyruvate.
quiz_met4:8.r: Pyruvate kinase is bypassed in two steps: pyruvate carboxylase makes oxaloacetate from pyruvate using ATP, then PEP carboxykinase makes PEP from oxaloacetate using GTP (p. 711).

quiz_met4:9.q: A child has the clinical picture of von Gierke disease, but glucose 6-phosphatase itself is normal. The defect is in the transporter that delivers glucose 6-phosphate to the enzyme. Into which compartment does this transporter normally move glucose 6-phosphate?
quiz_met4:9.r: Glucose 6-phosphatase sits in the endoplasmic reticulum. The G6P transporter (T1) moves glucose 6-phosphate from the cytosol into the ER lumen, where it is split to glucose and Pi (p. 702); a G6P transport defect is the rarer cause of von Gierke disease (p. 703).

1. Pentose phosphate pathway (LO 1)

2. Gluconeogenesis: definition, precursors, sites and conditions (LO 2)

6. Glycogen synthesis, glycogenolysis and their reciprocal regulation (LO 6)

Synthesis adds glucose from uridine diphosphate glucose (UDP-glucose) to non-reducing ends, breakdown removes it from the same ends with Pi, and phosphorylation switches the two enzymes in opposite directions (p. 696, p. 700, p. 706).
